posts.title: Bringing the fallen back to life
posts.description: How FreeBMD helped uncover the stories behind a school WW1 memorial What can happen when you combine military records, civilian records and a little determination? For Scott Paget and a group of former pupils of John Lyon School in Harrow on the Hill, the answer is a comprehensive digital archive that brings the stories of their First World War fallen back to life – with FreeBMD playing an important part in its development. From a brass plaque to a digital archive Scott, who had a brief volunteering spell with Free UK Genealogy as a programme manager earlier this year, was a pupil at John Lyon School between 1969 and 1974. He had wanted since 2019 to establish a permanent memorial to the school's fallen at St George's Memorial Church in Ypres, Belgium. The opportunity came when the school celebrated its 150th anniversary and Scott's former classmates, the class of 1976, marked their 50th anniversary. posts.title: Important security information from Free UK Genealogy
posts.description: Cyber security incident: Information for current and former volunteers This notice provides information about a cyber security incident affecting Free UK Genealogy, discovered on 2nd November 2026, and explains the precautions we recommend. It is intended for both current and former volunteers, including those who may be learning about the incident for the first time. Information relating to people who volunteered with us in the past may also have been affected. The findings and service arrangements described below reflect the position at the time this notice was published. Subsequent developments may be covered in later updates on our blog. What happened? On Monday 2nd November 2026, we discovered that an unauthorised user had gained access to part of our technical infrastructure, including systems connected to FreeBMD, FreeCEN and FreeREG. posts.title: Our data, new discoveries: how FreeBMD is helping researchers at the University of Cambridge
posts.description: FreeBMD's records are helping researchers at the University of Cambridge tackle one of the biggest challenges faced when trying to trace people through history: how to identify married women from one census to the next. The aim of the ‘Geolinking Project’ is to create links between people observed in different censuses, from 1851 to 1921, making it possible to build up a picture of their lives over time. Once completed, it will enable researchers to better explore family histories and people's lives in the context of wider historical changes. But tracing women’s lives is particularly challenging for a number of reasons, and this is where FreeBMD comes in. We spoke to Dr Alexis Litvine, project lead at the University of Cambridge, to learn more. Dr Alexis Litvine, Geolinking Project Lead, University of Cambridge, UK.
